answer.evidence: Every column scan shows the same two vertical gradients. Rows 1-6 run light to dark (the backrest face), and rows 7-12 repeat the same run (the seat face). Row 7 is a 1-row highlight at the top of the seat, but it is a cushion highlight, not a front-edge line under a top band. No band of rows reads as a horizontal seat surface seen from above. The rows 0-2 width steps (12, 14, 14) are just the rounded top corners of the backrest. The arms are drawn as vertical strips with no top plane. The whole piece is a face-on front elevation, and the seat surface is not seen from above.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate armchair is a tiny red piece with only 6 distinct colours in total, against 11-40 for the references. Its shading is shallow: a mid red, a light red highlight, a dark red-brown edge, and perhaps one more tone, so about 3 steps on the main red material against 5-6 in the Beodeul references. The outline is a dark red-brown tinted to the material (0% neutral edge pixels), which is correct and matches the Beodeul approach. The 5x5 flat-fill coverage is 0%, but only because the piece is small. By eye the cushion and arms are smooth, with no fabric grain, stitching, speckle or per-part shading, so it reads as flat and sticker-like. The median of 6 colours per tile is well below the hedge (10), stall (17) and well (20), and the 6 distinct colours is far below the 11-14 of even the simplest references (hedge, bench, lamp). A careful artist would not accept it next to the references because it looks thinner and flatter. It also lacks the multi-tone seat cushion, back and arm separation, and wooden feet detail that the references show.
